questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What the absence of labels removes
questions.stem: A field biologist has 5000 plant specimens with no species tags. What is missing for supervised learning?

options.text: A target variable for each specimen

questions.explanation: Supervised learning requires a target for each row. Without species tags, no target exists, so the setting is unsupervised. More data or a metric does not create labels.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a clustering objective minimises
questions.stem: In k-means, what quantity is minimised?
questions.explanation: k-means minimises the within-cluster sum of squared distances to centroids. Maximising between-cluster distance or optimising silhouette is a different goal.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A lower objective from a different starting point
questions.stem: Why can two k-means runs on the same survey data give different final objectives?

answer.exemplar: k-means is sensitive to initial centroids and can converge to different local minima. Different starting points lead to different clusterings and different within-cluster sums of squares.

questions.explanation: k-means converges to a local minimum that depends on initial centroids. Different starts can yield different clusters and objectives. Running multiple random starts mitigates this.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The assignment step in k-means
questions.stem: In one k-means iteration, the assignment step does what?

options.text: Assigns each point to nearest centroid

questions.explanation: The assignment step assigns each point to the nearest centroid. Recomputing centroids is the update step. k and standardisation are set beforehand.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The update step in k-means
questions.stem: In one k-means iteration, the update step does what?

options.text: Recomputes each centroid as its cluster mean

questions.explanation: The update step recomputes each centroid as the mean of its assigned points. Assignment happens first. k-means does not remove outliers or split clusters in a standard iteration.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Within-group sum of squared distances
questions.stem: Cluster points have squared distances to centroid 4, 1, 9, 2. What is the cluster WCSS?
questions.explanation: WCSS sums squared distances within the cluster: 4+1+9+2 = 16. It measures cluster compactness.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A starting centre placed on an extreme value
questions.stem: A k-means centroid starts on an extreme specimen. What is a likely consequence?
questions.explanation: An extreme initial centroid can isolate a single point, forming a singleton cluster. This often worsens the solution. It does not guarantee improvement or balance.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Two columns on incompatible scales
questions.stem: A survey has height in metres and weight in grams. Why standardise before k-means?

options.text: To prevent large-scale features dominating distance

questions.explanation: Without scaling, features with large numeric ranges dominate Euclidean distance. Standardisation puts features on comparable scales. It does not change k or handle missingness.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Two runs, raw columns and standardised columns
questions.learningObjective: Compare clustering on raw vs scaled
questions.stem: k-means on raw data gives one grouping; on standardised data, another. Which is more defensible for mixed units?
questions.explanation: With mixed units, standardised clustering avoids letting large-scale features dominate. Raw clustering is biased by units. The two are not identical, and clustering remains useful after scaling.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading a fall in the objective as k grows
questions.stem: As k increases, WCSS falls and then levels off. What does the bend indicate?
questions.explanation: The elbow where WCSS stops falling sharply suggests a reasonable k. It is not overfitting or underfitting, and a plateau does not mean no structure.
questions.hint: Look for the bend in WCSS.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: One unit's silhouette value
questions.stem: A specimen has silhouette score near 1. What does that indicate?

options.text: It is near a cluster boundary
It is well matched to its cluster

questions.explanation: A silhouette near 1 means the point is close to its own cluster and far from others. Near 0 means boundary; negative means likely misassigned.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a hierarchical method returns
questions.stem: What does hierarchical clustering produce?

options.text: A fixed set of k centroids

questions.explanation: Hierarchical clustering produces a dendrogram showing nested merges. It does not require k upfront and does not output only a score or one cluster.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What each linkage rule assumes about a merged cluster
questions.stem: Single linkage merges clusters based on which distance?

options.text: Minimum distance between any two points
Maximum distance between any two points

questions.explanation: Single linkage uses the minimum inter-cluster distance. Complete uses maximum, average uses mean, and centroid uses centre distance.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The second merge under average linkage
questions.stem: Clusters A and B have one pair distance 2 and one pair distance 4. What is the average linkage distance?
questions.explanation: Average linkage computes the mean of all cross-cluster pairwise distances: (2+4)/2 = 3. It is not the minimum or maximum.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: How many groups a dendrogram cut yields
questions.stem: A dendrogram has 12 leaves. Cutting at a height that separates 3 branches yields how many clusters?
questions.explanation: Cutting a dendrogram at a height that produces 3 branches yields 3 clusters. The number of leaves does not change the cut count.
questions.hint: Count the branches at the cut height.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading an objective curve across values of k
questions.stem: WCSS drops sharply from k=1 to k=3 then slowly. Which k is most plausible?
questions.explanation: The elbow at k=3 balances compactness with simplicity. k=1 ignores structure; k=10 overfits; k=0 is invalid. Choose the bend, not the minimum.
questions.hint: Choose the elbow, not the minimum.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Comparing silhouette values across values of k
questions.stem: Silhouette is highest at k=4 and lower at k=2 and k=6. Which k is preferred?
questions.explanation: Higher silhouette indicates better-defined clusters, so k=4 is preferred. k=2 and k=6 are weaker; k=1 is trivial.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A cluster centre read against an action
questions.stem: A cluster centroid has high mean leaf length and low mean petal width. How is this group best described?
questions.explanation: Clusters are described by their centroid profiles. A single specimen or count does not capture the group. Labels should follow features, not be arbitrary.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why the same data yields two groupings
questions.stem: Why might the same survey yield different clusters across two k-means runs?

answer.exemplar: k-means depends on random initial centroids and can settle in different local minima. Without fixing the seed or using k-means++, results vary across runs even on identical data.

questions.explanation: Random initialisation can lead to different local minima. Fixing the seed or using better initialisation improves reproducibility. The data itself need not change.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The steps of a k-means run
questions.stem: Order the k-means steps: choose k, assign points, update centroids, repeat until convergence.
questions.explanation: k is chosen first, then points are assigned, centroids updated, and the cycle repeats until convergence. Any other order breaks the algorithm.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Distances crowding together in many dimensions
questions.stem: In very high dimensions, why do nearest-neighbour distances become similar?
questions.explanation: In high dimensions, distances between points concentrate, so nearest and farthest become similar. This is the curse of dimensionality. Features do not become identical and clustering does not improve.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A projection chosen for maximum variance
questions.stem: PCA chooses components to maximise what?
questions.explanation: PCA finds directions of maximum variance. It is unsupervised and does not use labels, clusters, or centroids.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The loading of a variable on the first component
questions.stem: A variable has a large loading on PC1. What does that mean?
questions.explanation: A large loading means the variable contributes strongly to that component. It does not imply zero variance or removal. Small loading would indicate weak contribution.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Explained variance from eigenvalues
questions.stem: Eigenvalues are 6 and 4. What is the explained variance ratio of PC1?
questions.explanation: Total variance is 10, so PC1 explains 6/10 = 0.6. The ratio uses the eigenvalue divided by the sum of eigenvalues.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Total variance after standardising
questions.stem: After standardising 5 features, what is the total variance?
questions.explanation: Standardising each feature to unit variance gives total variance equal to the number of features, here 5. This is a property of standardisation.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Cumulative variance across kept components
questions.stem: Explained variance ratios are 0.5, 0.3, 0.2. What is cumulative variance for the first two components?
questions.explanation: Cumulative variance sums the ratios: 0.5 + 0.3 = 0.8. Keeping two components retains 80% of variance.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading a scree plot
questions.stem: A scree plot shows eigenvalues dropping then flattening after component 3. How many components to keep?
questions.explanation: The elbow after component 3 suggests keeping 3 components. Keeping all ignores parsimony; keeping 1 discards signal; keeping none is invalid.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading a loadings matrix
questions.stem: In a loadings matrix, variable height has loading 0.9 on PC1 and 0.1 on PC2. Which component is height associated with?
questions.explanation: The larger loading on PC1 means height is strongly associated with PC1. PC2 has a small loading. Neither or equal would ignore the magnitudes.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading a biplot
questions.stem: In a PCA biplot, two variable arrows point in opposite directions. What does that indicate?
questions.explanation: Opposite arrows indicate negative correlation between variables. Same direction indicates positive; perpendicular indicates near zero. Opposite does not mean identical.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Raw columns against standardised columns
questions.learningObjective: Compare PCA on raw vs scaled
questions.stem: PCA on raw mixed-unit data is dominated by which feature?
questions.explanation: Without scaling, PCA follows variance, so the largest-variance feature dominates. Standardisation prevents this. It is not random and not absent.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a factor is in a factor model
questions.stem: In factor analysis, what is a factor?
questions.explanation: A factor is an unobserved latent variable that explains correlations among observed variables. It is not observed, a centroid, or a PCA score, though related.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a stochastic embedding gives two pictures
questions.stem: Why can two t-SNE runs on the same data produce different maps?

answer.exemplar: t-SNE uses random initialisation and stochastic optimisation, so different runs can yield different embeddings. The global structure is not preserved, only local neighbourhoods.

questions.explanation: t-SNE is stochastic, with random initialisation and gradient descent. Different runs produce different layouts. It preserves local structure, not global distances.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Variance shares from singular values
questions.stem: Singular values are 3 and 1. What is the variance share of the first component?
questions.explanation: Variance is proportional to squared singular values: 9 and 1, total 10, so the first share is 9/10 = 0.9. Use squared singular values, not raw ones.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: How many components to keep for a downstream model
questions.stem: When using PCA before a classifier, how should the number of components be chosen?
questions.explanation: The number of components should be chosen by downstream performance, e.g. cross-validation. Keeping all defeats reduction; using one is too restrictive; random is invalid.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Explained variance is a statement about spread
questions.stem: What does explained variance in PCA describe?

options.text: How much of the total spread is captured

questions.explanation: Explained variance describes how much of the total spread in the data is captured by the components. It is not accuracy, clusters, or target correlation.
questions.hint: It is about spread, not prediction.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a flat map of high-dimensional data can show
questions.stem: What can a 2D embedding of high-dimensional survey data reliably show?
questions.explanation: 2D embeddings preserve local neighbourhoods, not exact global distances, causality, or original units. Overstating fidelity leads to wrong conclusions.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What distances in an embedding license
questions.stem: Can distances in a t-SNE map be interpreted as real data distances?
questions.explanation: t-SNE preserves local neighbourhoods, not global distances. Interpreting map distances as real distances is unsafe. 3D does not fix this.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The steps of a decomposition
questions.stem: Order PCA steps: standardise features, compute covariance, eigendecompose, project data.
questions.explanation: Standardise first, then compute covariance, eigendecompose, and project. Any other order is invalid. Projection requires components first.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading a decomposition before using it
questions.stem: Before using PCA components in a model, what should be checked?
questions.explanation: Check explained variance and loadings to ensure components capture signal. PCA is not automatically safe; sample size and cluster count are not the right checks.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Two runs of one embedding
questions.stem: How can reproducibility of a t-SNE map be improved?
questions.explanation: Fixing the random seed makes t-SNE reproducible. Output dimensionality, feature removal, or extreme perplexity do not address stochasticity.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What the absence of labels removes
questions.stem: Without labels, which task becomes impossible?
questions.explanation: Classification requires labels. Clustering, dimensionality reduction, and visualisation are unsupervised and do not need labels.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a clustering objective minimises
questions.stem: If a clustering objective minimises within-cluster variance, what does it avoid maximising?
questions.explanation: Minimising within-cluster variance does not directly maximise between-cluster separation, though they often move together. Sample size and feature count are not objectives.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A lower objective from a different starting point
questions.stem: How can the risk of a poor k-means local minimum be reduced?
questions.explanation: Multiple random initialisations reduce the chance of a poor local minimum. One centroid, less data, or k=1 do not help.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The assignment step in k-means
questions.stem: In standard k-means, assignment uses which distance?
questions.explanation: Standard k-means uses Euclidean distance for assignment. Cosine, Manhattan-only, or Hamming are variants or different methods, not the standard.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The update step in k-means
questions.stem: The centroid update computes what?
questions.explanation: The centroid is the mean of assigned points. Median or mode would define a different algorithm; random is invalid.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Within-group sum of squared distances
questions.stem: As k increases to n, what happens to WCSS?
questions.explanation: More clusters reduce WCSS; at k=n each point is its own cluster and WCSS is zero. It does not increase, stay constant, or go negative.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A starting centre placed on an extreme value
questions.stem: How can outlier sensitivity in k-means be reduced?
questions.explanation: k-medoids or robust scaling reduces outlier sensitivity. Increasing k to n, deleting large values, or ignoring distances are not sensible fixes.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Two columns on incompatible scales
questions.stem: Which scaling is common before distance-based clustering?

options.text: Standardisation to zero mean, unit variance

questions.explanation: Standardisation to zero mean and unit variance is common. No scaling lets large units dominate; min-max and log are alternatives but not the stated common default.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Two runs, raw columns and standardised columns
questions.stem: Why can scaling change the clusters found by k-means?

answer.exemplar: Scaling changes the relative distances between points, which changes nearest-centroid assignments. Since k-means depends on Euclidean distance, rescaling can alter the entire clustering result.

questions.explanation: k-means depends on Euclidean distance, so rescaling changes relative distances and assignments. The clustering can change substantially with different scales.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading a fall in the objective as k grows
questions.stem: Why not choose k that minimises WCSS?

options.text: It would set k to n

questions.explanation: Minimising WCSS always favours k=n, trivialising clusters. A useful k balances compactness and simplicity. k=1 maximises WCSS, not minimises it.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: One unit's silhouette value
questions.stem: A specimen has silhouette score -0.2. What does that suggest?

options.text: It may be assigned to the wrong cluster

questions.explanation: A negative silhouette suggests the point may be closer to another cluster than its own. It does not mean perfect clustering, centroid, or total failure.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a hierarchical method returns
questions.stem: Unlike k-means, hierarchical clustering does not require what?
questions.explanation: Hierarchical clustering builds a dendrogram without fixing k in advance. It still needs data and a distance metric, and it produces the dendrogram.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What each linkage rule assumes about a merged cluster
questions.stem: Complete linkage uses which inter-cluster distance?

options.text: Minimum distance between any two points
Maximum distance between any two points

questions.explanation: Complete linkage uses the maximum distance between points in two clusters. Single uses minimum, average uses mean, centroid uses centres.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The second merge under average linkage
questions.stem: Cross-cluster distances are 3, 5, 7. What is the average linkage distance?
questions.explanation: Average linkage is the mean of cross-cluster distances: (3+5+7)/3 = 5. It is not the min or max.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: How many groups a dendrogram cut yields
questions.stem: Cutting a dendrogram at a height that leaves 5 branches produces how many clusters?
questions.explanation: The number of clusters equals the number of branches at the cut height, here 5. Leaves do not determine this directly.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading an objective curve across values of k
questions.stem: WCSS falls 40% from k=1 to 2, 10% from 2 to 3, 2% after. Where is the elbow?
questions.explanation: The largest relative improvement ends at k=2, so the elbow is at k=2. k=3 adds little; k=10 overfits; k=1 ignores structure.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Comparing silhouette values across values of k
questions.stem: Silhouette peaks at k=3 with 0.62 and is 0.41 at k=5. Which k is preferred?
questions.explanation: Higher silhouette at k=3 means better-defined clusters, so k=3 is preferred. k=5 is weaker; k=1 is trivial; k=10 oversegments.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A cluster centre read against an action
questions.stem: A cluster of specimens has high mean soil moisture. What action follows?
questions.explanation: The centroid profile suggests the group is associated with high soil moisture, so treating them as moisture-loving is reasonable. Ignoring, random assignment, or deletion waste information.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why the same data yields two groupings
questions.stem: Which practice most improves k-means reproducibility?
questions.explanation: Fixing the random seed makes results reproducible. Changing k, shuffling only, or one initialisation do not ensure reproducibility.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The steps of a k-means run
questions.stem: When does k-means stop iterating?
questions.explanation: k-means stops when assignments (or centroids) no longer change, or a max iteration is reached. It does not require zero WCSS or cluster splitting.

provenance.author: bank-team-data-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used
